How Louisiana property tax works

Property tax here is built locally. Three parties share the work. The parish assessor values the property, parish residents vote on millage, and the sheriff typically mails and collects the bill. Assessment percentages are set by the state constitution, and appeals from local boards climb to the Louisiana Tax Commission.

Louisiana has parishes where most states have counties, so your contacts are the parish assessor and the sheriff, in New Orleans, Baton Rouge or a small town alike. East Baton Rouge's sheriff makes the point directly: the sheriff has no say in the size of your bill. Value comes from the assessor and the rate from local votes.

Assessment percentages

Land and the buildings on residential lots are assessed at 10% of fair market value, while other property is assessed at 15%. Those levels come from Article VII, section 18 of the Louisiana Constitution sets these levels, which also sets 25% for public service property other than land. The full text of section 18 is on the legislature's site.

Reappraisals happen on a cycle of four years or less. If one lifts a homestead-exempt house's assessed value by over 50% in a single year, the increase in tax is spread across four years. A sale cancels that cushion, so a buyer can owe the full amount that the long-time owner never did. The constitution also freezes the assessment level for qualifying owners, including those 65 or older, subject to an income limit.

Figuring a tax bill

The math is simple. Start with fair market value, take off any homestead exemption, apply the 10% level, and multiply what is left by the combined millage of your tax districts. Millage varies between parishes and between districts inside one parish. The assessor can tell you the rates for your address.

The exemption is a fixed amount, so every dollar of value above it is taxed in full. One more caution from the East Baton Rouge sheriff: the exemption reaches parish taxes only. City taxes and fire or crime fees are still owed on the full value.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Louisiana house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Homestead exemption

A homeowner can shield the first $75,000 of a home's market value from parish property tax, which equals $7,500 of assessed value. You must apply at the assessor's office, and the house has to be your primary residence.

  • One home per owner.
  • In East Baton Rouge Parish you need to own and live in the house by December 31 of the tax year.
  • City taxes and fire or crime district fees there are not reduced.
  • Losing the home in a tax sale can forfeit the exemption.

The benefit follows an owner-occupant. An investor or other buyer who will not live there would not qualify, so what you pay now may understate the next owner's bill. Be straight about that if a buyer asks.

Due dates and penalties

The year's taxes come due December 31. The roll normally gets to the collector by November 15, and bills go out in the last week of November.

  • Anything unpaid after December 31 is delinquent and accrues interest at 1% per month.
  • In East Baton Rouge the sheriff tacks on a collection fee once January 31 passes unpaid, then certified notice and advertising costs.
  • La. R.S. 47:2153 has the collector send certified mail by the first Monday of February, giving the owner 20 days before the lien goes to auction.
  • Bidders can be asked for a deposit of up to $1,000.

Under the newer process, the lien is auctioned first and the house later. The high bidder receives a recorded tax lien certificate. You stay the owner and stay in possession until a court judgment is carried out, and the lienholder cannot evict you or collect rent in the meantime. To clear the lien you repay the auction price plus interest of up to 1% a month, a 5% penalty and costs, at any point before enforcement action is filed.

Under the older tax sale process, a sold property could be redeemed within three years of recordation by paying a 5% penalty plus 1% interest a month. Parishes can differ, so call your sheriff's office to learn which one applies.

How to appeal your assessment

The order matters: assessor first, then the board of review, and only after that the Tax Commission and district court. Every stage has a short window.

StepDeadline or rule
Request a written notice of assessmentAsk no earlier than June 1; the assessor must receive it by June 15 (R.S. 47:1992)
Inspection of the roll15 days between August 15 and September 15 in most parishes; July 15 to August 15 in Orleans
Board of review complaintGive the board at least seven days' notice; the board may raise or lower the value
Appeal to the Tax CommissionHearings begin within ten days of receiving the certified lists (R.S. 47:1989)
District courtFile within thirty days of the commission's decision

Rolls go from the assessor to the board by October 1. The board has to hold hearings by September 15 and send its certified list to the Tax Commission by October 20. The commission may affirm, remand, reverse or modify an assessment. A taxpayer who sues pays the disputed amount under protest, while R.S. 47:1998 lets the undisputed part be paid without protest. The statutes are on Justia: R.S. 47:1992 and R.S. 47:1989.

Selling a Louisiana house when taxes are owed

The tax bill stays with the land. The sheriff will not divide it between buyer and seller, and any side deal you strike with the buyer is invisible to the collector. Tax, interest, penalties and fees remain due until somebody pays them.

Values are fixed as of January 1, so a sale later in the year can leave the old owner's name on that year's roll. An assessor may also add omitted property for up to three back years under R.S. 47:1966, so a house missing from the roll can trigger a catch-up bill.

  • Get the account balance from the sheriff's tax office before you list or sign.
  • Pay this year's bill at closing and write down how it was divided.
  • R.S. 9:2721 requires the deed to name who pays property taxes and where notices go, so check that line.
  • Ask the assessor whether the homestead exemption is active.

If back taxes are already piling up, we can look at the house as it stands and explain how the payoff would work at closing.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Louisiana homestead exemption?

It removes parish property tax on the first $75,000 of a primary residence's value, which is $7,500 of assessed value. You apply through the parish assessor. City taxes and fire or crime fees in East Baton Rouge are not covered.

When are Louisiana property taxes due?

Taxes are due by December 31 of the tax year. Bills are mailed in late November, and interest at 1% a month starts after December 31. A collection fee and advertising costs can follow after January 31.

What percent of value is a Louisiana home assessed at?

Land and residential improvements are assessed at 10% of fair market value under Article VII, section 18 of the Louisiana Constitution. Other property is assessed at 15%. Reappraisal happens at least every four years.

Can I sell my Louisiana house with back taxes owed?

Yes. The taxes are paid from the proceeds or by the buyer at closing, since they stay attached to the property. A recorded tax lien must be cleared before clean title passes, and the sheriff can give you a payoff figure.

How do I dispute my Louisiana assessment?

Ask the assessor for the notice, then bring a complaint to the parish board of review during its hearing window. A board decision can be appealed to the Louisiana Tax Commission, and then to district court within thirty days of the commission's decision.

title: Louisiana Homestead Exemption: Eligibility, Filing and Selling the Home

Louisiana Homestead Exemption: Eligibility, Filing and Selling the Home

We buy Louisiana houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

What the homestead exemption covers

The homestead exemption removes the first $7,500 of assessed value from the property tax base of an owner-occupied home. The amount is set by Article VII, section 20 of the Louisiana Constitution, which covers state, parish and special ad valorem taxes on a bona fide homestead.

A homestead can be a residence plus a field, pasture or garden on other tracts, as long as the total stays within 160 acres. A primary residence that is a mobile home qualifies even when the owner does not own the land, though the land itself gets no exemption in that case.

Residential improvements and land are assessed at 10 percent of fair market value under Article VII, section 18, so a $7,500 cut in assessed value lines up with roughly $75,000 of market value. What you actually save depends on the millage in your parish, which is why two owners of identical houses can see different dollar results.

Who qualifies

Section 20 limits the exemption to natural persons and to trusts that natural persons created for natural-person beneficiaries. A company cannot claim it, and neither can an owner who does not live in the house.

  • Surviving or former spouses who occupy the homestead keep the exemption if they hold title as owner, as usufructuary or through a testamentary trust.
  • Property held in indivision gets only the occupying owner's pro rata share.
  • Property bought on a bond for deed gets no exemption under the current text, with a carve-out for exemptions granted before June 20, 2003.
  • No person may receive more than one homestead exemption in the state.

The one-per-person rule matters if you own two houses. Selling the old one after you move does not create a second exemption, and the new home needs its own claim.

City and town taxes

Generally the exemption stops short of them. The constitution excludes municipal taxes, with an exception for Orleans Parish (state, general city, school, levee and levee district taxes) and for municipal taxes levied for school purposes.

So a homeowner inside a municipality may find the exemption saves less than the $7,500 figure suggests. Read the tax bill line by line, or ask the parish assessor which levies the exemption reaches.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Louisiana house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Keeping the exemption after a storm

A homeowner whose house was damaged or destroyed in a governor-declared disaster can keep the exemption during rebuilding. Under section 20(A)(10), an owner who cannot move back in by December 31 files an annual affidavit of intent to return, good for up to five years.

After that, the owner can keep the exemption for up to two more years if an insurance claim or a formal appeal is still pending, with official documentation. The assessor may then grant up to three more one-year extensions case by case.

If you plan to sell a storm-damaged house rather than rebuild, the exemption stops mattering once title passes, and the new owner starts fresh.

Age 65 freeze and disabled-veteran exemptions

These are separate from the homestead exemption, and each is filed with the parish assessor. The age-based assessment freeze is in section 18(G) of Article VII, and the disabled veteran exemptions are in section 21(K).

Related programs filed with the parish assessor
ProgramBenefit and conditions
Special assessment level (age 65 or older, certain disabled veteran owners and others)Assessment is held at the first qualifying year's total. Signed application to the assessor. Income cap of $100,000 until January 1, 2027, then $150,000. Ends December 31 of the year before the property is sold.
Veteran, 50% to under 70% service-connected disabilityNext $2,500 of assessed value exempt after the $7,500 homestead amount
Veteran, 70% to under 100%Next $4,500 of assessed value exempt
Veteran at 100% unemployability or total disabilityRemaining assessed value of the homestead exempt

Section 21 also describes an extra age-based exemption starting January 1, 2028, which needs voter approval in the parish or municipality. Count on it only if your parish confirms it was adopted.

Creditor protection is a separate rule

Louisiana has a second homestead concept in R.S. 20:1 that shields the home from seizure and sale by creditors. It works differently from the tax break.

  • It protects the first $35,000 in value of the homestead, and the full value when debts come from a catastrophic or terminal illness or injury that meets the statute's definition.
  • The protected land is up to 5 acres when the residence is in a municipality and up to 200 acres when it is not.
  • It covers the owner-occupant and the surviving spouse or minor children of a deceased owner.
  • It leaves out debts for the purchase price, taxes or assessments, rent carrying a privilege, mortgage advances, and work done to build or improve the home.

A waiver of this protection must be in writing, signed (by the spouse too, if the owner is married and not legally separated), and recorded in the mortgage records of the parish.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Louisiana houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How to claim it

File with the assessor in the parish where the house stands. The assessor's office is the authority on forms and timing. Louisiana has 64 parishes, each with one elected assessor.

Assessors generally grant retroactive exemptions for the last three years when an owner discovers a missed claim. An assessor may decline if a will is involved, so heirs who inherit a house should bring the succession paperwork along.

When you buy or inherit a house, remember R.S. 9:2721. A conveyance of immovable property filed with the parish recorder must name the person responsible for property taxes and give a mailing address for tax notices, and that person must give the information to the assessor.

Bring photo identification, proof that you live in the house, and the deed or succession paperwork. Ask whether the assessor wants anything else, since requirements can differ from one parish office to the next.

What a sale does to the exemption and the bill

A sale ends the seller's claim, and the buyer applies for a new one if the buyer will live in the house. The age freeze is even more direct: it generally expires December 31 of the year before the property is sold, and the house is then valued at fair market value.

Section 18(F) adds a wrinkle. When a reappraisal pushes the assessed value of homestead-exempt property up by more than 50 percent, the increase is phased in over four years, but the phase-in ends early when ownership transfers. A buyer can face a full reassessment sooner than the seller did.

Unpaid taxes follow the land. Ad valorem taxes are a charge on the immovable, tax sales are run under Article VII, section 25 and R.S. 47:2121 and following, and a debtor who redeems pays the taxes, costs, a 5 percent penalty and simple interest of 1 percent per month. The redemption period is three years from recording of the tax sale certificate, or 18 months for blighted property.

Checklist before listing or taking a cash offer

  • Confirm on your latest tax notice that the homestead exemption is applied. If it is missing, ask the assessor about back claims.
  • List any freeze, veteran or disability exemption you hold, because they end or change when title moves.
  • Check for unpaid taxes or a prior tax sale certificate recorded against the property.
  • Gather the succession judgment or affidavit if you inherited the house, since the assessor and any buyer will want to see how title reached you.
  • Ask the clerk of court or your closing notary which recording fees apply, since fees vary with the number of pages.

A cash buyer works through the same recording and tax steps as any other buyer, so these items should be tidy either way. If a house has a tax problem or a messy succession, say so early, because it affects how fast a sale can close.

Frequently asked questions

How much is the Louisiana homestead exemption?

It is $7,500 of assessed value on an owner-occupied home. Homes are assessed at 10 percent of market value, so that matches about $75,000 of market value, and the actual savings depend on your local millage.

Can I claim a homestead exemption on a rental house?

No. The exemption is for a bona fide homestead that the owner occupies, and only one is allowed per person in Louisiana. A landlord can claim it only on the home where they actually live.

Does the homestead exemption transfer to the buyer when I sell?

No. It belongs to the owner who occupies the home, so the buyer files a new claim with the assessor. The age 65 assessment freeze also ends when the house is sold.

Does the exemption stop a creditor from forcing a sale?

Not by itself. The tax exemption and the creditor protection in R.S. 20:1 are separate rules, and the creditor protection has its own limit of $35,000 and a list of debts it leaves out, such as the purchase price and unpaid taxes.

Do I keep the exemption if a hurricane makes my house unlivable?

Yes, in many cases. Under section 20(A)(10) you file an annual affidavit of intent to return, which can protect the exemption for up to five years, with further extensions in some situations.

title: Louisiana Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling
content:
Louisiana Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling

Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Louisiana Estate and Inheritance Tax sale

Selling a Louisiana House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Louisiana?
We buy Louisiana houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Does Louisiana have an estate or inheritance tax?

No. Nothing is owed to the state on a Louisiana estate today. The inheritance tax was repealed, and the estate transfer tax only ever existed to capture a federal credit that no longer exists.

Act 822 of the 2008 Regular Session repealed the inheritance tax law in R.S. 47:2401 to 2426, and since January 1, 2012 no inheritance tax receipts are issued, whatever the date of death. The estate transfer tax in R.S. 47:2431 to 2437 equaled the federal credit for state death taxes. That credit was replaced by a deduction for deaths after December 31, 2004, so no state estate transfer tax is due for those deaths.

For heirs of a Louisiana house, the sale proceeds are not reduced by a state death tax. The money questions that remain are federal, plus the cost and time of moving title.

The estate transfer tax return

One filing rule is still on the books. R.S. 47:2436 requires an estate transfer tax return where tax is due or where the deceased's net estate is $60,000 or more. The heirs or legatees file it, and it goes to the collector of revenue and to the person designated as tax collector under R.S. 47:2417.

The deadline is nine months after death, or before a United States estate tax return is filed, whichever comes first. The return lists the deceased's full name, residence at death, estate value, whether a federal return was filed, safety deposit box contents omitted from the estate and any omitted assets, with an explanation.

Whether a return is still expected on an estate with no tax due is a question for the succession attorney or a CPA, since the $60,000 trigger remains in the statute.

Federal estate tax in 2026

Only large estates owe federal estate tax. The basic exclusion amount for people who die in 2026 is $15,000,000, raised to that level by the Working Families Tax Cuts law signed July 4, 2025. The annual gift exclusion for 2026 is $19,000 per donee. An estate under the exclusion amount owes no federal estate tax, and the filing threshold for a 2026 death is also $15,000,000.

Death-related taxes that may touch a Louisiana estate
Tax or filingWhere it stands
Louisiana inheritance taxRepealed, no receipts since Jan. 1, 2012
Louisiana estate transfer taxNone due for deaths after Dec. 31, 2004
Estate transfer tax return (R.S. 47:2436)Required if net estate is $60,000 or more
Federal basic exclusion, 2026 death$15,000,000
Federal annual gift exclusion, 2026$19,000 per donee
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Louisiana house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Income tax when an heir sells

An heir's gain is usually figured from the home's value on the date of death, not from what the deceased paid. Inherited property generally takes the fair market value on the date of death as its basis, whether or not the executor files a federal estate tax return.

That is why a house inherited and sold soon afterward often produces little or no taxable gain. Any gain is the sale price less the stepped-up basis and allowed selling costs. Two situations deserve a closer look:

  • Community property: when either spouse dies, the full value of community property, even the survivor's half, generally becomes the basis of the entire property.
  • Special valuation: for some farm or business property, and for property valued under estate tax rules, the basis can follow that valuation instead.

Keep the date-of-death appraisal. If no estate tax value is reported, the appraised value at death used for state inheritance or transmission tax purposes can establish basis, so a written valuation helps in any case.

Getting legal title to sell

Heirs cannot sell just because the owner died. Title has to be moved to them through a succession. Louisiana does this through a court proceeding that ends in a judgment of possession, or through a sworn affidavit when the estate qualifies as a small succession.

Under Code of Civil Procedure art. 3062, a judgment of possession is prima facie evidence of the relationship of the parties it recognizes, as heir, legatee, surviving spouse in community or usufructuary, and of their right to possess the estate. A title company will look for that judgment or equivalent paperwork before it insures a sale.

Louisiana treats a surviving spouse differently from most states. Under Civil Code art. 890, when descendants survive, the spouse has a usufruct over the decedent's share of the community property, to the extent the decedent has not disposed of it by will. The usufruct ends when the spouse dies or remarries. Because a usufruct is an interest in the house, it has to be addressed in the sale paperwork.

Skipping court with a small succession affidavit

Some estates do not need to be opened in court. Code of Civil Procedure art. 3431 lists three situations:

  • A person domiciled in Louisiana who died intestate.
  • A person domiciled in Louisiana who died testate leaving no immovable property in Louisiana, if the surviving spouse and all persons who would inherit, with or without the testament, agree to waive probate.
  • A person domiciled outside Louisiana who died intestate or whose testament was probated by court order of another state.

Under art. 3432, at least two persons sign a sworn affidavit, including the surviving spouse if there is one and at least one heir. With no surviving spouse, at least two heirs sign, and if there is only one heir, a second person with actual knowledge signs too. The affidavit gives the date of death and domicile, marital status, the heirs and their relationships, a description of the property sufficient to identify immovable property for transfer, the value of each item and the total, and each heir's interest.

An heir who does not sign must either be unlocatable after reasonable diligence or have received thirty days' written notice by U.S. mail without objecting. Signing the affidavit also accepts the succession for that heir, so families should understand the estate's debts first.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Louisiana houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Taxes, mortgage and utilities while the estate is open

Those bills keep running whether or not a succession has been opened, so the heirs or the sale proceeds cover them. For a vacant Louisiana house, a few steps help:

  • Keep insurance active, and ask the carrier how a vacant house is treated.
  • Notify the lender and the parish assessor's office of the death if mail is going to the old address.
  • Photograph the condition of the house and keep copies of repair bills in case an executor or other heir questions the sale price.

Where heirs disagree, a cash offer will not settle the dispute, but a signed judgment or affidavit gives everyone one version of who owns what.

Selling for cash from an open estate

A cash buyer can close once title is in the hands of the people entitled to sell, so the first step is the same as for any buyer: prove authority. Expect to provide the judgment of possession or the filed affidavit, a copy of any will, and payoff information on liens.

Many heirs live out of state and cannot clear out a house, cut the grass or fix storm damage from a distance. Selling as-is spares them those chores. A call with an estate attorney or CPA before closing is time well spent, mostly to plan what to do with the proceeds.

Frequently asked questions

Does Louisiana charge an inheritance tax?

No. Act 822 of 2008 repealed it, and no inheritance tax receipts have been issued since January 1, 2012, regardless of date of death.

Does Louisiana have a state estate tax in 2026?

No state estate transfer tax is due for deaths after December 31, 2004, because the federal credit it relied on was replaced by a deduction.

What is the federal estate tax exemption for a death in 2026?

$15,000,000, under the law signed July 4, 2025.

Is the sale of an inherited house in Louisiana taxable?

Only the gain above the stepped-up basis is taxable. Inherited property generally takes its date-of-death value as basis, so little gain is common when the sale follows soon after.

Do I need a court case to sell my parent's house in Louisiana?

Not always. A small succession affidavit works when art. 3431 allows it, such as for an intestate Louisiana domiciliary. Estates with a will covering Louisiana land generally need a judicial succession.

Louisiana eviction, step by step

A Louisiana eviction is a fast, summary court case that starts only after a written notice to vacate has gone unanswered. The steps follow the Code of Civil Procedure, title XI, which governs the eviction of tenants and occupants.

  1. The lessor or owner delivers a written notice to vacate (art. 4701 or 4702).
  2. If the tenant or occupant does not comply, the owner has the court cite them to appear by a rule to show cause why possession should not be delivered (art. 4731). The rule states the grounds.
  3. The court makes the rule returnable no earlier than the third day after service, tries it and hears any defense (art. 4732(A)).
  4. If the owner wins, or the tenant fails to answer or appear, the court renders a judgment of eviction immediately (art. 4732(B)).
  5. If the tenant has not complied within twenty-four hours, the court issues a warrant to its sheriff, constable or marshal to deliver possession to the owner (art. 4733).

Our companion guide on the eviction notice covers step one in detail. This page starts at the courthouse.

Which court hears an eviction?

A justice of the peace court can hear a residential eviction, and so can the parish or district court. Code of Civil Procedure art. 4912 gives justice of the peace courts jurisdiction, shared with the parish or district court, over suits by landowners or lessors to evict occupants or tenants of leased residential premises, whatever the monthly or yearly rent.

The article also reaches some commercial and farm leases. A justice of the peace court may hear evictions of tenants of leased commercial premises and farmland where monthly rent does not exceed $5,000, again regardless of the rent due or the rent for the rest of the lease.

Which courthouse an owner uses depends on where the house sits. In a parish with city courts, parish courts or justice of the peace wards, the clerk of court can tell you where an eviction rule is filed.

Timing of each stage

The statute sets short minimum windows, and real calendars depend on the court. These are the numbers to plan around.

Statutory time limits in a Louisiana eviction
StageTime allowed
Notice to vacate (art. 4701)At least 5 days from delivery
Hearing on the rule (art. 4732(A))Not earlier than the third day after service
Judgment of eviction (art. 4732(B))Effective for not less than 90 days
Voluntary compliance (art. 4733)Within 24 hours of the judgment
Suspensive appeal request and bond (art. 4735)Within 24 hours of the judgment

Add up the minimums and the fastest lawful path takes more than a week from delivery of the notice. That assumes the owner files promptly and the court has an open hearing slot.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Louisiana house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What happens at the hearing

The judge tries the rule on the day it is returnable and hears any defense the tenant raises. Bring the lease if there is one, the written notice with proof of when it was delivered, and a record of what is owed.

A tenant who fails to answer or appear loses by default. Under art. 4732(B), the court renders a judgment of eviction immediately if the owner is entitled to relief or the lessee or occupant fails to answer or appear. That judgment is effective for not less than ninety days, which gives the owner time to carry out the order rather than a single day.

Owners who are family members, heirs or buyers should bring documents showing they now hold the lessor's position. Art. 4704 defines lessor to include an assignee or transferee, so title paperwork matters.

Can a tenant appeal?

Yes, but an appeal does not stop the eviction by itself. Under art. 4735, execution of the judgment is suspended only if the defendant answered the rule under oath pleading an affirmative defense that would entitle them to keep possession, applied for the appeal, and filed the appeal bond within twenty-four hours after the judgment.

The court sets the amount of the suspensive appeal bond, enough to protect the appellee against damage from the appeal. For the owner, that twenty-four hour window usually decides whether the warrant for possession can issue.

What a landlord cannot do during an eviction

An owner who skips the court process risks a penalty. Under art. 4731(C)(2), a lessor's failure to follow that article lets a residential lessee recover $500 or twice the monthly rent, whichever is greater, and the tenant may seek a restraining order or injunction. The court may award costs and attorney fees to the prevailing party.

After a federally declared disaster, the same article adds thirty days of protection for residents of the declared parishes: a household that has left the home is not treated as having abandoned it during that time. For a Louisiana seller whose rental was hit by a hurricane or flood, that affects whether the house can be treated as vacant.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Louisiana houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Does selling a rented house end the lease?

No. Civil Code art. 2711 provides that transfer of the leased thing does not terminate the lease unless the lessor and lessee agreed otherwise. The buyer arrives with the tenant already in the house.

Whether the buyer is bound by the lease turns on recording. Under art. 2712, a third person who acquires an immovable subject to an unrecorded lease is not bound by it, and the lessee, absent a contrary clause in the lease, has an action against the lessor for losses caused by the transfer. R.S. 9:2721 goes the other way for recorded leases: a buyer of property subject to a recorded lease that is not divested by the acquisition takes the property subject to all its provisions, including any provision for paying a commission to a leasing agent.

Before listing, find out whether the lease was ever recorded in the parish conveyance records, and what it says about rent, term and early termination.

The tenant's security deposit in a sale

The deposit moves with the property. Under R.S. 9:3251(B), when the lessor's interest is transferred during the lease, the transferor must also transfer the deposit to the successor, and the transferor is then relieved of further liability for it. The new owner becomes responsible for returning it when the lease ends.

The general rule in subsection (A) requires return to a residential tenant within one month after the lease ends. The landlord may keep what is reasonably needed to remedy a default or unreasonable wear, and if any is kept, an itemized statement with reasons is due within that month. The tenant must give a forwarding address, and the one-month rule does not apply where the tenant abandons the premises.

Write the deposit amount into the sale paperwork so it is credited correctly at closing.

Finish the eviction before selling?

It depends on the lease, the case and how much time you have. Finishing the eviction clears the house for showings, but it takes court time and may mean cleanup of what the tenant leaves behind.

Owners weighing the choice usually compare:

  • Cost and time of finishing a case, including repairs after the tenant leaves.
  • Whether the lease is recorded and would bind a buyer under R.S. 9:2721.
  • Whether the tenant is paying and wants to stay, which changes the picture entirely.
  • A sale as-is with the tenant in place, which passes the lease and the deposit to the buyer under the rules above.

We also look at houses that come with tenants or a difficult rental history. A Louisiana attorney can advise on a specific lease.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

How long does a Louisiana eviction take after the notice period?

The court may set the hearing no earlier than the third day after service of the rule. If the owner wins, the tenant has twenty-four hours to comply before a warrant issues. Actual timing depends on the court's calendar.

Which court handles evictions in Louisiana?

Justice of the peace courts share jurisdiction with parish or district courts over residential evictions under art. 4912, whatever the rent.

How long is a Louisiana judgment of eviction good for?

At least ninety days, under art. 4732(B). That gives the owner time to obtain a warrant and have possession delivered.

Does an appeal stop a Louisiana eviction?

Only in narrow cases. The tenant must have answered under oath pleading an affirmative defense, and must apply for the appeal and file the bond within twenty-four hours of the judgment.

Does the lease end if I sell my rented Louisiana house?

No. Civil Code art. 2711 says transfer of the leased thing does not terminate the lease unless the parties agreed otherwise. A recorded lease binds the buyer under R.S. 9:2721, while an unrecorded lease does not bind a third-party buyer under art. 2712.

content:
Louisiana Quitclaim Deed: Recording, Fees and When It Works

Cash Home Buyers in Louisiana
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Louisiana Quitclaim Deed: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Louisiana Quitclaim Deed sale
  • Turn the Louisiana Quitclaim Deed offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Louisiana House? Get a Cash Offer

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Louisiana?
We buy Louisiana houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

Is there a quitclaim deed in Louisiana?

Not by that name. Louisiana law has no form called a quitclaim deed. The nearest equivalent is Civil Code article 2502, which lets a person transfer whatever rights he has in a thing without warranting that those rights exist.

Under that article the transferor owes no refund of the price if the transferee is later evicted, and the transfer cannot be rescinded for lesion. Louisiana is a civil law state, so deed vocabulary comes from the Civil Code. The Orleans Parish clerk describes a deed as an Act of Sale, which may take the form of a Cash Sale, Credit Sale or Warranty Deed.

So expect the paper you sign to carry a Civil Code title such as act of sale, not the words quitclaim deed.

What a transfer without warranty does and does not do

The buyer receives the seller's rights as they stand and carries the risk that they are weaker than hoped. Article 2502 adds a few more points for anyone choosing this route.

  • The transfer raises no presumption that the buyer acted in bad faith.
  • It counts as a just title for acquisitive prescription, so a buyer who then holds the land can build toward ten years of possession.
  • If the seller later acquires ownership of the thing, that later title does not pass to the buyer.
  • The seller does not guarantee a refund of the price if a third party wins the property.

A full sale works differently. Under article 2503 the warranty against eviction is implied in every sale, and the parties may enlarge or limit it. Even when they exclude it, the seller must return the price after an eviction unless the buyer clearly knew of the risk, declared the purchase to be at his own risk, or the refund duty was expressly excluded. A seller is always liable for an eviction caused by his own act, and a contrary agreement is void.

Article 2500 defines eviction as the buyer's loss, or danger of losing, all or part of the thing sold because of a third party's earlier right, including undisclosed encumbrances.

Form requirements

A transfer of immovable property must be made by authentic act or by act under private signature, under article 1839. An oral transfer can bind the parties only in narrow cases, where the property was delivered and the transferor admits the transfer under oath.

An authentic act under article 1833 is a writing executed before a notary public or other authorized officer and two witnesses. The parties, witnesses and notary all sign, and a party who cannot sign makes a mark at the notary's direction. Closings usually run through a notary for that reason.

  • Effect against third persons begins only when the deed is filed in the parish (C.C. art. 1839).
  • The deed must name the person responsible for taxes and a notice address (La. R.S. 9:2721).
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Louisiana house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Where a Louisiana deed is recorded

File the deed with the clerk of court, acting as recorder, in the parish where the property sits. Until it is filed there, the instrument does not bind third persons.

Orleans Parish shows how the process runs. Its Land Records Division at 1340 Poydras Street accepts documents by mail, in person or through eRecording vendors, and a cover sheet tells the office to record in the mortgage records, the conveyance records, or both. Clerk staff cannot tell you which documents to file.

Any deed filed in Louisiana must name the person responsible for taxes and give a mailing address for tax notices. That person passes the details to the assessor so bills reach the right place.

Parish clerks set their own hours, payment methods and add-on charges, so call before mailing a check.

Recording costs

La. R.S. 13:844 sets the base fee at $100 for one to five pages, $200 for six to 25 pages and $300 for 26 to 50 pages, plus $5 for each page above 50.

ServiceFee
Recording, 1 to 5 pages$100
Recording, 6 to 25 pages$200
Recording, 26 to 50 pages$300
Each name indexed after ten$5
Mortgage certificate, first name$20, then $10 per name
Cancelling a single mortgage$50

The base fee covers indexing up to ten names and one certified copy. A document recorded in both the mortgage and conveyance records is charged separately for each, and paper other than 8.5 by 11 or 8.5 by 14 inches adds $20 a page.

Orleans Parish adds a $5 remote access portal fee and a $30 courthouse building fund fee per recording. The city also charges a $325 documentary transaction tax on sales. Other parishes have their own add-ons.

Orleans Parish filing rules

The Orleans clerk's Land Records Division will reject or surcharge documents with bad margins, and it does not take personal checks.

  • The first page needs a two inch top margin, and every page needs one inch at the bottom and both sides, or a $20 surcharge applies.
  • The first page must carry a caption naming the type of act, in type no smaller than eight point.
  • By mail, send a business check or money order payable to Clerk of Court.
  • eRecording is available through CSC, ePN and Simplifile.
  • A cover sheet marks the document for the mortgage records, the conveyance records or both.

A recorded sale there also triggers the documentary transaction tax of $325 per taxable document, which falls on the seller. It is paid at recording or billed, and a bill unpaid after 30 days adds interest and a $500 penalty.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Louisiana houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

When a transfer of rights works for a seller

It can suit a transfer between family members, a cleanup of a boundary or interest, or a case where the seller honestly cannot vouch for title. It fits poorly when the buyer pays full price and needs title insurance.

  • Heirs who have not finished a succession may hold only uncertain rights.
  • A divorce settlement can move one spouse's interest to the other.
  • A buyer who needs the seller to stand behind the title should ask for a full sale with the implied warranty left in place.

Moving title does not erase a mortgage, tax lien or judgment. A recorded mortgage stays on the record until a cancellation is filed, and Orleans Parish charges $50 to record the cancellation of a single mortgage.

If you want to sell a house with unclear title, an inherited share or a lien, we can read the record with you and explain what a closing would need.

Frequently asked questions

Is a quitclaim deed valid in Louisiana?

Louisiana has no deed by that name, but article 2502 of the Civil Code lets you transfer the rights you hold without warranting them. The recorded paper is usually an act of sale, donation or transfer of rights, and it must meet the form rules for immovable property.

Does a Louisiana deed need a notary?

A transfer of immovable property can be an authentic act or an act under private signature. An authentic act is signed before a notary or other authorized officer and two witnesses, which is why most closings use a notary.

Where do I record a deed in Louisiana?

File it with the clerk of court in the parish where the property is located. The instrument affects third persons only from the time it is filed there. In Orleans Parish that is the Land Records Division at 1340 Poydras Street.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Louisiana?

The base fee is $100 for one to five pages, $200 for six to 25 pages and $300 for 26 to 50 pages. Orleans Parish adds a $5 portal fee and a $30 building fund fee, and other parishes may add their own charges.

Does the seller still warrant title with a no warranty transfer?

Not for the rights themselves, since under article 2502 no refund is owed if the buyer is evicted. The seller stays liable for his own acts, because article 2503 voids any agreement excusing an eviction he caused.

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Louisiana Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property sale
  • Turn the Louisiana Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Louisiana House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Louisiana?
We buy Louisiana houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Succession: Louisiana's version of probate

Louisiana calls probate a succession. The goal is a judgment of possession, or in a small estate an affidavit, that shows who now owns what the decedent left. The petition goes to the district court for the parish where the person was domiciled at death. In Orleans Parish that is the Civil District Court.

If the decedent lived outside Louisiana, a succession can be opened in any parish where the person owned immovable property, such as a house. Before you list an inherited home, find out which parish court or clerk of court holds the file.

Small succession dollar limits

A small succession covers an estate with a gross value of $200,000 or less at the date of death, when the decedent was domiciled in Louisiana. Code of Civil Procedure art. 3421 sets that limit and a second tier for ancillary successions.

SituationGross value limit
Decedent domiciled in Louisiana$200,000 or less at date of death
Decedent domiciled elsewhere, Louisiana property only (ancillary)$125,000 or less at date of death
Death at least 20 years before the affidavit is signedNo dollar limit

Some older guides still give $125,000 as the general cap. Check the date on anything you read.

Who can use the affidavit instead of going to court?

Article 3431 allows a small succession without opening a court case in three situations. Each is narrower than it first sounds.

  • A Louisiana domiciliary who died without a will.
  • A Louisiana domiciliary who died with a will but left no immovable property in the state, and only if the surviving spouse and every person who would inherit with or without the will agree to waive probate.
  • A non-domiciliary who died without a will, or whose will was probated by court order in another state.

Someone who left a will and owned a Louisiana house falls outside the second item, since a house is immovable property. That estate needs a judicial succession. Paragraph B of the same article also lets a governor-appointed public administrator use the affidavit for small estates with no heir present, after a single advertisement in the official parish journal and no notice of opposition.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Louisiana house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What goes in the small succession affidavit

Article 3432 covers the affidavit for an estate with no will. At least two people must swear to it. With a surviving spouse, the spouse signs along with one or more heirs. With no spouse, two heirs sign, or one heir and a second person who knows the facts if there is only one heir.

  • Date of death, domicile, marital status and last residence of the decedent.
  • Each heir's name, last known address and relationship, and the reason any heir did not sign: could not be located after reasonable diligence, or was given 30 days' notice by mail and did not object.
  • A description of the property, labeled community or separate, detailed enough to transfer an immovable.
  • The value of each item and the total at death, each heir's interest, and any usufruct of the surviving spouse.
  • A statement, sworn under penalty of perjury, that each signing heir accepts the succession.

Article 3433, added by Acts 2024, No. 90, covers a non-domiciliary who died with a will. It adds a copy of the will, a certified copy of the other state's probate order, and the legatee's acceptance.

Recording the affidavit to move title to a house

Record the affidavit, or a certified copy, in the conveyance records of the parish where the house sits. Under article 3434 a recorded affidavit is admissible and is prima facie evidence of what it states, including the heirs' relationship to the decedent and their rights in the property.

Banks and others holding the decedent's money or property can rely on a multiple original or certified copy as authority to pay or deliver to the named successors, and they are discharged when they do.

Anyone left out of the affidavit has a window to object. A person who claims to be a successor but was not named has two years from the recording date to assert an interest against a third party who acquired the property for value, or that party's successors. Recording in the right parish matters for another reason: under Civil Code art. 3338 and R.S. 9:2721, an unrecorded instrument has no effect on third persons, and the recorded conveyance must name who pays property tax and give a mailing address for tax notices.

When a court-run succession is needed

You need a judicial succession when the facts fall outside the affidavit rules: a will that must be probated, a house in a testate estate, or an estate above the dollar limit. The aim is a judgment of possession that recognizes the heirs or legatees and puts them in possession.

For an intestate estate with little debt, Code of Civil Procedure arts. 3001 through 3008 allow an ex parte petition for possession by all competent heirs who accept the succession. It usually comes with an Affidavit of Death, Domicile and Heirship under arts. 2821 and 2822, signed by two people with knowledge. Civil Code art. 962 presumes a successor accepts unless there is a written renunciation, which is why filings normally include every successor.

For a testate estate, art. 3031 lets the court put legatees in possession on an ex parte petition from all general and universal legatees. The will must be probated, each legatee must be competent or represented and must accept, and no creditor may have demanded administration. A will must be probated within five years of the judicial opening of the succession under art. 2893, and a succession representative named in the will joins the petition for possession.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Louisiana houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Can a succession representative sell the house?

Yes, by private sale if the court approves. Under Code of Civil Procedure art. 3281, the representative files a petition describing the property, the price and conditions, and the reasons for a private sale, and attaches any sale agreement already signed.

The representative may sign the agreement first, as long as it is conditioned on court approval. The petition is due within 30 days after signing.

For heirs in a hurry, this means a buyer can sign a contract while the court paperwork runs. Closing waits on the approval.

Selling an inherited house as an heir

Two problems come up most: proving who owns the house, and paying carrying costs while the paperwork runs.

  • Surviving spouse protections: homestead rights under R.S. 20:1 reach the surviving spouse and minor children of a deceased owner, and the constitutional homestead exemption can continue for a surviving spouse who lives in the home.
  • Property taxes: the tax is a charge on the land, so unpaid balances travel with the house. Redeeming after a tax sale costs the taxes, a 5 percent penalty and 1 percent simple interest per month.

A cash buyer still needs the heirs' ownership documents to close, so finish the affidavit or judgment first if you can. A buyer who purchases as-is also takes over the repair work that stalls many inherited sales.

Frequently asked questions

Do I have to go through court to inherit a house in Louisiana?

Not always. If the decedent lived in Louisiana, died without a will, and left an estate of $200,000 or less, a small succession affidavit under arts. 3431 and 3432 can work. A will plus a house usually means a judicial succession.

How much is a small succession in Louisiana?

$200,000 or less in gross value for a Louisiana domiciliary, and $125,000 or less for an ancillary succession of someone domiciled elsewhere. A death at least 20 years before the affidavit has no dollar limit under art. 3421.

Who signs a small succession affidavit?

At least two people. With a surviving spouse, the spouse signs plus at least one heir. With no spouse, two heirs sign, or one heir and another person who knows the facts.

Where is the affidavit recorded?

In the conveyance records of the parish where the house is located, under art. 3434. Banks and others holding the decedent's money may also rely on a certified copy to pay the named heirs.

Can I sell the house before the succession is finished?

A succession representative can sign a private sale agreement before court approval, but the contract is conditioned on the court approving it. The petition must be filed within 30 days of signing.
